title: Derivatives of Inverse and Inverse Trig Functions
subject: AP Calculus AB

chunks.text: The graph of an inverse function f⁻¹ is the reflection of the graph of f across the line y = x, which swaps the roles of input and output.
Reflecting across y = x swaps rise and run, so a slope of m on the original function becomes a slope of 1/m on the inverse at the corresponding point; inverse slopes are reciprocals.
The inverse function derivative rule is (f⁻¹)'(a) = 1/f'(f⁻¹(a)), valid when f is differentiable and one-to-one and f'(f⁻¹(a)) ≠ 0.
To apply the inverse rule you do not evaluate f' at a; you first find f⁻¹(a), the input that f maps to a, and evaluate f' there, then take the reciprocal.
The inverse rule comes from differentiating f(f⁻¹(x)) = x with the chain rule: f'(f⁻¹(x))·(f⁻¹)'(x) = 1, so (f⁻¹)'(x) = 1/f'(f⁻¹(x)).
If f has a horizontal tangent at a point (derivative zero), its inverse has a vertical tangent there and the inverse derivative is undefined.
To compute (f⁻¹)'(a): find the value b with f(b) = a, compute f'(b), then take the reciprocal 1/f'(b).
Example: for f(x) = x³ + x + 1, solving x³ + x + 1 = 3 gives x = 1, so f⁻¹(3) = 1, and (f⁻¹)'(3) = 1/f'(1) = 1/(3·1² + 1) = 1/4.
The number-one inverse-derivative error is evaluating f' at a instead of at f⁻¹(a); the original derivative must be evaluated at the matching input.
A common AP setup gives a table of x, f(x), and f'(x) and asks for (f⁻¹)'(c): find the row where f(x) = c, read f' in that row, and take the reciprocal.
The derivative of arcsin x is 1/√(1 − x²).
The derivative of arccos x is −1/√(1 − x²), the same magnitude as arcsin's derivative but with a negative sign because arccos is decreasing.
The derivative of arctan x is 1/(1 + x²), which is defined for all real x and always positive, so arctan is increasing everywhere.
The inverse trig derivatives are algebraic, containing no trigonometric functions in the answer.
The arcsin and arccos derivatives are undefined at x = ±1, matching the vertical tangents at the endpoints of those graphs.
With the chain rule, d/dx[arctan(g(x))] = g'(x)/(1 + [g(x)]²) and d/dx[arcsin(g(x))] = g'(x)/√(1 − [g(x)]²).
Example: d/dx[arctan(3x)] = 3/(1 + 9x²), since the inner derivative of 3x is 3.
Example: d/dx[arcsin(x²)] = 2x/√(1 − x⁴), using the chain rule with inner derivative 2x.
Example: d/dx[arcsin(2x)] = 2/√(1 − 4x²), where the inner factor 2 must not be forgotten.
The arcsin derivative is derived by setting y = arcsin x so sin y = x, differentiating implicitly to get cos y·(dy/dx) = 1, then using cos y = √(1 − x²) to obtain dy/dx = 1/√(1 − x²).
The arctan derivative is derived from tan y = x by differentiating to sec²y·(dy/dx) = 1, giving dy/dx = 1/sec²y = 1/(1 + tan²y) = 1/(1 + x²).
The expressions 1/(1 + x²) and 1/√(1 − x²) reappear as antiderivatives in integration, where they integrate to arctan x and arcsin x respectively.
